docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
Put one or more files per genome in a directory, named <genome>.<anything>:

Files Mode What happens grape.gff3.gz + grape.dna.fa.gz genome longest coding transcript per gene, CDS spliced and translated (prep genome) grape.gff3.gz + grape.cds.fa.gz [+ grape.pep.fa.gz] gff+cds longest transcript per gene; the GFF attribute matching the FASTA names is found automatically grape.bed + grape.cds / grape.pep processed used as given; the BED may be in MCScanX layout

FASTA files are classified by their names (cds, pep, protein, dna, genome, ...) or, if the name does not tell, by their content. A sample sheet (--samples, columns species, gff, genome, bed, cds, pep) overrides the detection. Protein records are matched to the genes through their headers (transcript:, gene:, .CDS / -P suffixes); when they do not match, proteins are translated from the CDS.

docs.title: Steps
docs.text:
1. inputs: data/<genome>.bed/.cds/.pep.
  2. orthology: OrthoFinder when installed (--orthofinder auto, the default; yes to require it): orthogroups, orthologues, gene trees and a rooted species tree. Otherwise (no) MCscan3's own: DIAMOND all-against-all, MCL orthogroups, reciprocal best hits.
  3. synteny: ortholog run for every pair of genomes and each genome against itself.
  4. soi: the Orthology Index of every block; soi/<a>.<b>.soi.anchors keep orthologous synteny (--soi-cutoff).
  5. pan: pan-genes linked by anchors that are orthologous synteny and in one orthogroup, completed with the other members of their orthogroups (<genome>_nonsyntenic columns), and a riparian plot.
  6. network: synteny network, clusters, profiles and a network species tree; the trees are compared and disagreements reported.
  7. ancestral: ancestral gene orders at every node of the species tree, ancestral chromosomes painted on every genome, and all karyotypes on the tree.
  8. dup: duplicate-gene classes of every genome.
  9. wgd (--ks): anchor-pair Ks (MCscan3's LPB93 estimator: no PAML needed), block-median Ks and mixture models per genome.
  10. wgd-consensus (--ks): WGDs placed on the species tree by consensus of four lines of evidence (WGD guide).
  11. report: report.html.

The species tree matters

Ancestral genomes and WGD placement depend on the rooted species tree. With few genomes, or genomes with WGDs, OrthoFinder's and the synteny-network trees can both be wrong (on six eudicots neither matched the accepted tree). The report flags disagreements; give a trusted tree with --tree species.nwk when it matters.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
results/
  run.json            what ran: status, time and notes of every step, and the results shown in the report
  samples.tsv         what was found
  data/               prepared <genome>.bed/.cds/.pep
  orthology/          OrthoFinder results or MCscan3's own orthogroups
  synteny/            ortholog run per pair (.last, .anchors, .lifted.anchors, dot plots)
  soi/                Orthology Index per block, .soi.anchors
  pan/                pangenes.tsv, riparian.png
  network/            net.edges/.clusters/.profile.tsv, net.tree.nwk
  ancestral/          anc.<node>.cars.tsv, <node>.karyotype.png, tree.karyotype.png
  dup/                <genome>.<class>.pairs, <genome>.genes
  wgd/                <genome>.anchor.ksd.tsv, .blocks.tsv, .blocks.png, consensus.tsv/.png
  report_files/       figures and interactive dot plot data used by the report
  report.html

Steps that fail are listed in the report and in a table printed at the end of the run; the others still run. Re-running the same command skips finished work.

docs.title: Re-running some steps
docs.text:
--steps re-runs only the steps named; the results of the others are kept from run.json:

mcscan3 pipeline run genomes/ -o results --steps ancestral,report --tree species.nwk
mcscan3 pipeline report results          # only rebuild report.html (e.g. after an update)

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
report.html is one self-contained page (no internet access needed; share the whole results/ directory or just report.html with report_files/). It has:

  • summary cards: genomes, genes, orthogroups, orthologous blocks, pan-genes, ancestral CARs and WGDs placed;
  • interactive dot plots of every genome pair and every genome against itself: pick a pair, scroll to zoom, drag to pan, click a chromosome name to zoom to it, hover a dot for its two genes, block, orientation and Orthology Index; colour by orientation, block or Orthology Index; download the view as PNG;
  • pan-genes (core, shell, private), riparian plot, synteny network and species trees, ancestral karyotypes on the tree, duplicate-gene classes as stacked bars, Ks mixtures and WGDs on the species tree;
  • the run: every step with its status and time, and every note.

Figures open full size on click and tables sort by clicking a column header. The page follows the system's light or dark mode, with a toggle.

Report of six eudicot genomes (amborella, Arabidopsis, grape, peach, poplar, soybean).

docs.title: Run time
docs.text: Six plant genomes (27,000-56,000 genes each) on 10 CPUs: OrthoFinder is the longest step (hours on a laptop; much less on a server); synteny for 21 pairs takes about 30 minutes; the other steps minutes each; --ks adds anchor Ks of every genome (native LPB93: minutes) and the WGD consensus.

docs.title: Two themes
docs.text:
Every plot command takes --theme:

  • mcscan3 (default): white panels, a colour-blind-safe palette (Okabe-Ito, Paul Tol), viridis as the default colour map, figures cropped to their content, and plot-specific improvements (below);
  • classic: the original JCVI look, pixel for pixel (MCscan3 tests its figures against JCVI's). MCSCAN3_THEME=classic makes it the default for every command.
Plot With --theme mcscan3 plot dotplot blocks coloured forward / inverted; the second genome's chromosomes ordered and flipped along the first (--order auto); every dot drawn (rasterised); chromosomes as light bands with short names (Chr01 -> 1); unplaced scaffolds (under 0.5% of the genes) hidden, with a note; --oi greys out older duplications plot karyotype ribbons coloured by the first genome's chromosomes (--color-by chr), by ancestral chromosome (car) or by any gene table (labels); --genomes a,b,c builds the layout; --auto-order reduces crossings; chromosome names on white tabs, readable over ribbons plot ks, ks report step outline over a light fill, plain numeric ticks, fitted peaks marked with their Ks plot heatmap white cell borders, values printed in matrices of up to 400 cells plot blastplot horizontal short chromosome names, light separators, unrotated ticks plot ribbon, microsynteny, tree, chromosome; phylo draw cropped to the drawing; tree axes hidden plot riparian (always) small scaffolds left out, chromosomes reordered, small blocks fainter

Figures that are new in MCscan3 (Ks mixtures, WGDs on the tree, ancestral karyotypes, riparian plots, networks, subgenomes) always use the MCscan3 style: a bold left-aligned title with a grey subtitle that states the method and the numbers behind the figure.

docs.title: Colour themes
docs.text:
The drawing style above (--theme) is separate from the colour theme, which every figure of every command takes from the global options before the command:

mcscan3 theme list                                   # the themes, with their colours
mcscan3 --plot-theme slides plot dotplot a.b.anchors ...
mcscan3 --plot-theme paper --plot-font Arial karyotype map ...
mcscan3 --plot-theme muted --colormap magma ks report ...

Theme For light the default house style dark slides and screens on black midnight deep blue background, Tol's light colours paper journals: black text, Okabe-Ito, small type, fine lines slides talks: 35% larger type, heavier lines, Tol's bright colours vibrant, muted, ibm other colour-blind-safe palettes, each with its own colour maps print colours that also survive black-and-white printing grey greyscale only

Every built-in palette is ordered so that neighbouring colours stay apart for protanopia, deuteranopia and tritanopia. Colour maps that colour-blind readers cannot read (jet, rainbow, turbo, red-yellow-green, spectral) are replaced by every named theme (--plot-set safe_colormaps=false keeps them); the default theme keeps a map chosen on the command line and warns instead. A figure that needs more colours than a theme has continues with the house colours, never repeating one.

docs.title: Change anything
docs.text:
For one run, over the theme:

Option Changes --palette muted or --palette '#0072B2,#E69F00,#009E73' categorical colours --colormap cividis sequential colour map --diverging PuOr_r diverging colour map --background '#fdf6e3' background --plot-font Arial, --font-scale 1.2 type --plot-set line_scale=1.5 --plot-set ink=#222222 any theme field --plot-set '#D55E00=#B2182B' one colour, wherever it appears --formats svg,tiff, --plot-dpi 600, --transparent output files

Or keep your own theme in a file and use it everywhere:

mcscan3 theme init lab.toml --base paper    # every field, commented
mcscan3 theme check lab.toml                # colour-blind and contrast check
export MCSCAN3_PLOT_THEME=$PWD/lab.toml     # every later run, and the desktop app

base = "paper"
categorical = ["#0072B2", "#E69F00", "#009E73", "#CC79A7"]
sequential = "cividis"

[colors]                 # swap any colour of any figure
"#D55E00" = "#B2182B"

[commands."plot dotplot"]   # one command (or [commands.karyotype] for a group)
sequential = "magma"

mcscan3 theme check '#E69F00,#D55E00,#009E73' checks any list of colours, and mcscan3 theme preview muted lab.toml -o compare.png draws the same specimen in each theme. In the desktop app, Settings > Figure colours sets the theme of every job.

docs.title: Flexible figures
docs.text: MCscan3 figures are modern by default and flexible on request: every layout decision that the program makes for you (which chromosomes, in what order, which way round, at what scale) can be overridden from the command line, so a figure can be shaped for a paper without editing it by hand.

docs.title: Dot plots: order, flip and zoom
docs.text:
--qorder (x axis) and --sorder (y axis) take a comma-separated list of chromosomes. A trailing - draws a chromosome reversed, and chrom:start-end keeps only that range (10M, 250k allowed). Chromosomes left out are not drawn, so the same options zoom on a fusion or a fission:

mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.poplar.anchors --qorder 14 --sorder 2,14,5-         # grape 14 vs three poplar chromosomes
mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.poplar.anchors --qorder 5:10M-25M --sorder 2:0-12M  # two regions

Without them, the y axis is ordered and flipped along the x axis automatically (--order auto). Reversed chromosomes carry a minus after their name (5−).

docs.title: Riparian plots: scale, merging and manual order
docs.text: Option Effect (default) all rows on one scale (genes, or base pairs with --basepair), each row centred --fill every row stretched to the full width --merge-gap N blocks of one chromosome pair fewer than N genes apart become one braid: a macrosynteny view --min-block N leave out blocks of fewer than N anchors --chrom-order GENOME=5,2-,9 fix the chromosomes of one row, their order and direction (repeatable) --no-reorder keep the natural order of every row (by default rows follow their neighbour and flip) --highlight FILE, --region G:chr:start-end trace QTL or other regions through every genome

docs.title: Karyotypes and paintings to scale
docs.text:
plot karyotype --genomes a,b draws horizontal tracks on one scale and centred (--fill for the old full-width tracks). plot painting draws the chromosomes of one genome as ideograms to base-pair scale, painted by the chromosomes of another: the MCScanX bar plot redrawn as a karyotype.

mcscan3 plot painting grape.poplar.anchors --qbed grape.bed --sbed poplar.bed --min-block 10 -o poplar.painting.pdf

docs.title: Trees of karyotypes and WGDs
docs.text:
ancestral tree-karyotype draws karyotype evolution from the ancestor at the top down to the species, with clades on pastel regions (--clade Rosids=ath,poplar, repeatable), full species names (--label ath="Arabidopsis thaliana"), WGDs as red circles and every rearrangement drawn as inputs → outputs (EEJ, NCF, RCT, FIS). macro ancestors (BUSCO ancestral linkage groups) draws the same tree. wgd consensus --label names the species on the WGD tree.

Each figure is shown in the gallery.

docs.title: Chromosome names
docs.text: Figures label chromosomes with short names: Chr01 becomes 1, and a prefix shared by all sequences (NC_0449) is dropped. Accessions such as CP126648.1 say nothing about the chromosome, so mcscan3 prep genome writes <prefix>.chroms.tsv beside the BED with the names of the FASTA descriptions or of the GFF region lines (CP126648.1 chr1). Every figure that reads that BED then shows 1. The sequence ids themselves stay unchanged. For genomes prepared another way, write the two-column file by hand.

docs.title: Interactive dot plots
docs.text:
Give plot dotplot an output name ending in .html for an interactive dot plot: scroll to zoom, drag to pan, click a chromosome name to zoom to it, hover a dot for its two genes and its block. The page is self-contained and opens in any browser, offline.

mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.peach.lifted.anchors -o grape.peach.html
mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.peach.lifted.anchors --oi grape.peach.oi -o grape.peach.html  # + Orthology Index

The pipeline report has one for every pair of genomes. Try one in the gallery.

Fonts that cannot draw very small labels (macOS Helvetica at 5 pt or less) are replaced automatically.

docs.title: The figures of MCscan3
docs.text: Figure Command Dot plot of two genomes (or one against itself), zoomed or reordered plot dotplot (--qorder, --sorder) Chromosomes painted by the synteny of another genome plot painting Macrosynteny across genomes plot karyotype, plot riparian Local synteny with gene glyphs plot microsynteny Ks histograms plot ks, plot histogram, wgd mix --plot, wgd peaks --plot Ks of several genomes / transcriptomes wgd compare WGDs on the species tree wgd consensus Transcriptome summary wgd transcriptome (<prefix>.summary.*) Ancestral chromosomes painted on genomes ancestral karyotype Karyotype evolution on the species tree, rearrangements drawn ancestral tree-karyotype, macro ancestors Biased fractionation subgenome fractionation Subgenomes painted on the polyploid subgenome assign Network heatmap, profile, graph, cluster network plot Synteny depth histogram synteny depth --histogram, plot depth Trees, heatmaps, chromosome painting, BLAST dot plots plot tree, plot heatmap, plot chromosome, plot blastplot

docs.title: Gallery
docs.text:
mcscan3 plot gallery -o gallery          # every plot type in both themes, next to JCVI's original
open gallery/index.html

See also Figures.

docs.title: Biased fractionation
docs.text:
After a polyploidy many duplicated genes are lost. When one subgenome keeps more genes than the other(s), fractionation is biased, a sign of allopolyploidy and subgenome dominance.

mcscan3 ortholog run ath brapa --quota 1:3          # B. rapa is a mesohexaploid relative to Arabidopsis
mcscan3 subgenome fractionation ath.brapa.lifted.1x3.anchors --ref-bed ath.bed --poly-bed brapa.bed \
    --copies 3 -o brapa --format png

The reference must not share the polyploidy. Each block of the polyploid covers an interval of the reference; its retention is the share of the reference genes in that interval that the block kept. At every reference gene the covering blocks are ranked by retention: LF (least fractionated), MF1, MF2...

Ranking by retention alone makes LF look better than MF even without any bias, so the significance test shuffles which copies kept each gene (keeping how many) and re-ranks (--permutations). Outputs: brapa.genes.tsv (the polyploid gene of each rank per reference gene), brapa.blocks.tsv (retention and rank of each block), brapa.windows.tsv and a figure of retention along the reference chromosomes.

docs.title: Assigning chromosomes to subgenomes
docs.text:
With progenitor-like diploids (or their closest living relatives), every polyploid gene votes for the progenitor whose syntenic partner is closest; votes are smoothed along the chromosomes:

mcscan3 ortholog run bnapus brapa
mcscan3 ortholog run bnapus bole
mcscan3 subgenome assign bnapus --progenitor brapa=bnapus.brapa.lifted.anchors \
    --progenitor bole=bnapus.bole.lifted.anchors -o bnapus --format png

Closeness is the anchor score, or Ks with --ks NAME=FILE (wgd ksd tables). Votes closer than --margin abstain. Homoeologous exchanges show as segments of the other subgenome within a chromosome. For scaffold-level assemblies use --min-frac 0 (keep every scaffold) and a smaller --min-run. Outputs: bnapus.genes.tsv, bnapus.segments.tsv, bnapus.chromosomes.tsv (subgenome and confidence per chromosome) and a karyotype figure coloured by subgenome.

See Validation for B. rapa, maize and B. napus.

docs.title: Phasing without progenitors, and the circos summary
docs.text:
subgenome phase phases a polyploid from itself (self-synteny, --copies = number of subgenomes) or against an unduplicated reference. It runs homoeologous sets, subgenome-specific k-mers, LTR retrotransposons, homology and Ks to progenitors when given, a consensus, retention and a circular summary:

mcscan3 fetch genome csat=GCF_030686135.1 -o camelina          # Camelina sativa, 2n = 6x = 40
mcscan3 pipeline inputs camelina -o camelina/prep              # BED, CDS, proteins, chromosome names
cd camelina/prep
mcscan3 ortholog run csat csat --cpus 8                        # self-synteny
mcscan3 ks kaks csat.csat.lifted.anchors --cds csat.cds -o csat.kaks.tsv --cpus 8
mcscan3 subgenome phase ../csat.dna.fa.gz --bed csat.bed --self csat.csat.lifted.anchors \
    --copies 3 --cpus 8 -o phase/csat
mcscan3 subgenome circos phase/csat --bed csat.bed --anchors csat.csat.lifted.anchors \
    --ks csat.kaks.tsv --key right -o csat.circos.pdf

subgenome circos works for any number of subgenomes. The rings, numbered from the outside in and drawn only when their input exists, are:

  1. the consensus subgenome, window by window, with homoeologous exchanges marked (▲);
  2. one thin ring per line of evidence, showing the subgenome it calls in each window;
  3. the windows significantly enriched for one subgenome's k-mers;
  4. the share of each subgenome's specific k-mers, one ring per subgenome;
  5. the subgenome-specific LTR retrotransposons;
  6. all intact LTR retrotransposons;
  7. gene density;
  8. gene retention.

In the centre, syntenic blocks between subgenomes are coloured by subgenome pair. The insets show the insertion ages of the specific LTR retrotransposons and the Ks of the blocks of each pair. Chromosome names come from <bed>.chroms.tsv (written by pipeline inputs) or from --names. --key right puts the key beside the circle, for a landscape figure.

docs.title: Orthology across genomes that share a polyploidy
docs.text:
When several genomes share one polyploidy, subgenome orthology matches their copies subgenome by subgenome. Every gene of an unduplicated reference becomes a pillar: its surviving copies in each genome, one slot per homoeologous track. A gene-loss model on the species tree, with one loss rate per subgenome, scores how the slots map to subgenomes. A hidden Markov model along the reference keeps neighbouring pillars in the same arrangement unless synteny breaks. The output gives every pillar's orthologs with a posterior, the loss rates (the fractionation bias, tested against equal rates), and how many losses happened before and after each speciation.

The Brassiceae triplication, shared by Brassica rapa and B. oleracea, with Arabidopsis thaliana as the reference (anchors from ortholog run ath brapa --quota 1:3):

mcscan3 ortholog run ath brapa --quota 1:3
mcscan3 ortholog run ath bole --quota 1:3
mcscan3 subgenome orthology --ref-bed ath.bed --copies 3 \
    --genome brapa=ath.brapa.lifted.1x3.anchors:brapa.bed \
    --genome bole=ath.bole.lifted.1x3.anchors:bole.bed -o brassica

Across 22,021 pillars, the least fractionated subgenome (LF) kept 75.7% of the genes in B. rapa, MF1 52.1% and MF2 32.3%, with loss rate weights of 0.43, 0.95 and 1.62. The likelihood-ratio test against equal loss rates gave P < 10⁻³⁰⁰. Most losses came before the two species split: 0.59 losses per gene, against 0.12 and 0.11 on the branches to B. rapa and B. oleracea. On simulated pillars with a known history, 95–99% of the arrangements were recovered, and 99.9–100% of those with a posterior of at least 0.95.

docs.title: Pairwise synteny
docs.text: The quick start walks through grape vs peach step by step. This page explains the choices along the way.

docs.title: The one-command pairwise run
docs.text:
mcscan3 ortholog run grape peach --cpus 8

ortholog run aligns the two gene sets (LAST on CDS by default; --dbtype prot uses proteins, --align-soft diamond_blastp|blast another aligner), filters the hits (tandem merging, C-score --cscore), finds colinear blocks (--dist, --min-size) and recovers extra anchors by liftover. It writes:

  • grape.peach.last, grape.peach.last.filtered: the hits;
  • grape.peach.anchors, grape.peach.lifted.anchors: the blocks;
  • grape.peach.pdf: a dot plot.

The same steps can be run one by one: align last, filter cscore / filter blastfilter, synteny scan, synteny liftover.

docs.title: Polyploidy and copy ratios
docs.text:
A genome with a WGD has several syntenic copies of each region of an unduplicated relative.

mcscan3 synteny depth grape.poplar.anchors --histogram    # e.g. 1:2
mcscan3 ortholog run grape poplar --quota 1:2             # keep at most 1 grape and 2 poplar blocks per region
mcscan3 quota align grape.poplar.anchors --quota 1:2 --screen

quota align solves a linear programme so that each region of the first genome is covered at most once and of the second at most twice (the ploidy ratio).

docs.title: Orthologous synteny
docs.text:
Older duplications make paralogous synteny: blocks between a region and the copies of its ortholog's duplication. The Orthology Index (OI) of a block is the share of its anchors that are orthologues:

mcscan3 ortholog soi grape.poplar.lifted.anchors --orthologs OrthoFinder/Orthologues -o grape.poplar.soi.anchors
mcscan3 ortholog soi grape.poplar.lifted.anchors --blast grape.poplar.last -o grape.poplar.soi.anchors   # RBH as orthologues

Blocks with OI at least --cutoff (0.6) are kept. soi also writes <anchors prefix>.oi, the OI of every block (numbered in the order of that anchors file). Orthologous synteny is what pan-genes, ancestral genomes and the WGD consensus use.

docs.title: Figures
docs.text:
mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.poplar.lifted.anchors --theme mcscan3              # forward / inverted blocks
mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.poplar.lifted.anchors --oi grape.poplar.lifted.oi --theme mcscan3   # older duplications grey
mcscan3 plot karyotype --genomes grape,peach,poplar --anchors-dir . --theme mcscan3   # no layout files needed

With --theme mcscan3, dot plots order and flip the second genome's chromosomes along the first (--order auto), so blocks fall on the diagonal and inversions stand out; karyotypes colour ribbons by the first genome's chromosomes (--color-by chr), order chromosomes to reduce crossings, and can colour by ancestral chromosome (--color-by car). See Plotting and themes.

docs.title: Tips
docs.text:
• Use the same gene names in the BED and FASTA files; --no-strip-names keeps transcript suffixes such as .t01.
  • Scaffold-level assemblies: --skipempty drops scaffolds without anchors from dot plots; karyotype and riparian plots leave out sequences with few genes (--min-frac).
  • A genome against itself (ortholog run grape grape) finds its duplicated blocks, the input of anchor-pair Ks and duplicate classification.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: How MCscan3's results are checked.

docs.title: Parity with JCVI
docs.text: The 78 ported features are tested against the output of JCVI v1.6.7 on real genomes (grape, peach, poplar from Ensembl Plants): text outputs byte for byte, figures pixel for pixel (tests/golden). 4 features are kept as legacy-only. See Deviations for JCVI defects found and how MCscan3 handles them.

docs.title: New features: known answers
docs.text: Every new feature is tested on simulated data with a known answer (tests/features), for example: a simulated history of fusions, fissions and inversions recovered by ancestral genomes; biased and unbiased fractionation (calibrated: 2/40 false positives at the 5% level, 10/10 biases of 0.85 vs 0.60 found); a simulated WGD at Ks ~0.6 recovered from a simulated transcriptome.

docs.title: Ka/Ks against PAML
docs.text:
On identical codon alignments (40 grape paralog pairs):

MCscan3 PAML Agreement gy94 codeml (pairwise, F3x4) r = 0.99998 (largest dS difference 0.03) lpb93 yn00 (LPB93) r = 0.9995 ng86 yn00 (NG86) median dS difference 0.6%

Genome scale: 11,742 grape anchor pairs in 27 s (lpb93) or 4 min (gy94) on 10 CPUs.

docs.title: Real genomes
docs.text:
WGDs on the species tree (wgd consensus; Amborella, grape, Arabidopsis, poplar, peach, soybean; Ensembl Plants):

Known event Placed on Lines of evidence gamma triplication core-eudicot stem 4/4 Arabidopsis alpha and beta Arabidopsis 3/4 salicoid WGD poplar 3/4 Glycine and legume WGDs soybean 4/4

No WGD was called for grape, peach or Amborella.

Fractionation and subgenomes:

Data Result Published B. rapa vs Arabidopsis LF 60.5%, MF1 46.3%, MF2 39.6%, p = 0.005 the same ordering (Wang et al. 2011; Cheng et al. 2012) maize vs sorghum maize1 53.9%, maize2 38.6%, p = 0.005 maize2 more fractionated (Schnable et al. 2011) B. napus vs B. rapa and B. oleracea 99.2% of genes on the right subgenome (smoothed), 96.8% of scaffolds A/C subgenomes from the gene names

Transcriptomes without a genome (wgd transcriptome, NCBI TSA assemblies):

Species Peaks (Ks) Known WGDs Arabidopsis 0.75, 1.91 alpha, beta maize 0.24, 0.93, 2.10 maize WGD, grass rho, older soybean 0.08, 1.92 Glycine WGD, gamma; the legume WGD (~0.6) is not resolved from the paranome

Ancestral genomes: on the six eudicots, the core-eudicot ancestor resolves into 18 ancestral chromosomes (21 published post-gamma protochromosomes); most grape chromosomes paint as one or two ancestral chromosomes.

Synteny network: 47 of 51 genomes of the SynNet demo set (7.4 million syntenic links); the network tree recovers the grasses, Brassicaceae, legumes and Rosaceae.

docs.title: Ks of gene pairs
docs.text:
MCscan3 has its own Ka/Ks estimators, and can also run PAML:

Method Command option Speed Notes lpb93 --method lpb93 ~0.1 ms / pair Li (1993), Pamilo & Bianchi (1993); corrects transition bias. A good default ng86 --method ng86 ~0.02 ms / pair Nei & Gojobori (1986) gy94 --method gy94 ~60 ms / pair maximum likelihood (Goldman & Yang 1994), as pairwise codeml yn00 --method yn00 slow PAML yn00 (needs MUSCLE, PAL2NAL, PAML) codeml --method codeml slow PAML codeml

Times are after the codon alignment (about 4 ms per pair). All native methods run in parallel with --cpus.

mcscan3 ks kaks grape.grape.anchors --cds grape.cds --method lpb93,gy94 --cpus 8 -o grape.kaks.tsv

Saturation

Ks above about 3 is unreliable for every method. Maximum likelihood (gy94, codeml) gives very large values for near-random pairs (protein identity below ~0.3) where counting methods give moderate ones; ks kaks --min-identity 0.3 leaves such pairs out, and the WGD commands use --max-ks (default 5).

docs.title: Ks distributions of a genome
docs.text:
There are three kinds, from the noisiest to the cleanest WGD signal:

# 1. paranome: all paralog pairs, in families, each duplication counted once
mcscan3 wgd ksd grape.cds --blast grape.grape.last -o grape.paranome.tsv --method lpb93 --cpus 8
# 2. anchor pairs: syntenic duplicates only (from a self comparison)
mcscan3 wgd ksd grape.cds --anchors grape.grape.lifted.anchors -o grape.anchor.tsv --method lpb93 --cpus 8
# 3. block medians: one Ks per syntenic block
mcscan3 wgd blocks grape.anchor.tsv -o grape.blocks.tsv --max-ks 3 --bed grape.bed

Block medians are the steadiest: all anchors of a block come from one duplication.

docs.title: Finding the peaks
docs.text:
mcscan3 wgd mix grape.blocks.tsv --model all --plot grape.mix.pdf     # GMM, ELMM, Bayesian GMM; best by BIC
mcscan3 wgd peaks grape.blocks.tsv --log --plot grape.peaks.pdf       # kernel density peaks
  • GMM: log-normal components, one per WGD.
  • ELMM: an exponential for the steady stream of small-scale duplicates near Ks 0, plus log-normal WGD components (wgd v2's model). Best for paranomes.
  • Bayesian GMM (bgmm, needs [stats]): chooses its number of components itself.

--bootstrap gives confidence intervals of the peaks, --assign the component of every pair. wgd mix reports possibly saturated peaks near --max-ks.

docs.title: WGDs on the species tree
docs.text:
wgd consensus places WGDs on the branches of a rooted species tree where at least --min-support (2) of four independent lines of evidence agree:

  1. block ratio: the synteny depth of each genome against a genome without the events;
  2. quota ratio: the copy ratio at which quota alignment stops gaining anchors;
  3. Ks: block-Ks peaks placed against rate-corrected speciation Ks (each genome's own branch length since a split, from orthologous Ks with an outgroup, as in ksrates);
  4. gene trees: where the syntenic paralogs of each Ks peak coalesce in the gene trees (e.g. OrthoFinder's resolved gene trees), the method of PUG. Gene trees are rooted on the outgroup's genes; each pair's last common ancestor is mapped to the species tree when both of its child clades hold at least half the species below it; each gene tree votes once per event and node. This places each event by itself, whatever the rates of evolution.

The gene trees also check the Ks peaks. Pairs of a real WGD are spread over many gene families, about one gene tree for every 2 to 10 pairs. A mixture component made of tandem arrays or a few large families puts thousands of pairs into a handful of trees. A peak with fewer than --min-tree-rate (0.05) gene trees per pair is rejected, and it gets no Ks vote either. A peak whose placement is split between two adjacent branches is flagged as possible allopolyploidy (see subgenome assign). Without syntenic paralogs, duplication bursts of the reconciled gene trees are counted instead (Tree2GD-style).

The number of WGDs on a branch is the median count over the lines that saw events. Ks peaks less than 1.35 times apart count as one event (a mixture often splits a broad peak in two), and the Ks and gene-tree counts are capped by the copy ratios when those saw events on the branch.

On six eudicots (Amborella, Arabidopsis, grape, peach, poplar, soybean) with OrthoFinder's gene trees, this calls the γ triplication at the core-eudicot stem, α and β in Arabidopsis, two WGDs in soybean, the salicoid WGD in poplar, and none in grape or peach. It also rejects a grape Ks component at 0.35: 7,594 pairs in only 60 gene trees.

Copy ratios are chained from the outgroup through the nearest less-duplicated genome and split into x2 (duplication) and x3 (triplication) events by parsimony on the tree.

mcscan3 wgd consensus species.nwk --bed-dir data --anchors-dir synteny --cds-dir data \
    --blocks-dir wgd --soi-dir soi --outgroup amborella \
    --gene-trees OrthoFinder/Resolved_Gene_Trees/Resolved_Gene_Trees.txt --cpus 8 -o wgd/consensus

It writes consensus.tsv (per branch: each line of evidence, support, calls), consensus.events.tsv (per Ks peak: its branch by Ks and by gene trees, gene trees per pair, votes, share and status), consensus.evidence.tsv (per genome: multipliers and Ks peaks, and the rejected ones), consensus.pair_ks.tsv and a figure. ancestral tree-karyotype --wgd consensus.tsv draws the calls on the karyotype tree. pipeline run --ks runs all of this.

Related: wgd tree-map (duplications from gene trees alone; --paralogs pairs.tsv --outgroup X places your own pairs gene1<TAB>gene2<TAB>event), wgd correct (rate-correct one speciation Ks onto a genome's scale).

docs.title: Transcriptomes (no genome)
docs.text:
mcscan3 wgd transcriptome trinity.fasta -o sample --cpus 8 --format png

Longest ORFs per transcript, isoforms and alleles collapsed (--collapse, 97% identity), DIAMOND paralog families, node-weighted Ks with the native estimators (--method), and mixture models. It writes sample.ksd.tsv, sample.mix.tsv, sample.ks.png and a four-panel sample.summary.png (Ks with the mixture, Ka/Ks against Ks, ORF lengths, family sizes).

Note

Paranomes resolve clear WGDs well, but a subtle older peak next to a very recent WGD can be absorbed by the small-scale duplicates (soybean's legume WGD near Ks 0.6; see Validation). Synteny resolves such cases when a genome is available.

docs.title: Comparing genomes and transcriptomes
docs.text:
mcscan3 wgd compare ath=ath.ksd.tsv soybean=soybean.ksd.tsv maize=maize.ksd.tsv -o compare --format png

Stacked Ks distributions on one axis with each sample's peaks, so shared WGDs line up.

docs.title: Analyses explained
docs.text:
These pages explain why each MCscan3 analysis works, not only how to run it. Every page follows the same plan:

  1. The question the analysis answers.
  2. The logic: what MCscan3 does, step by step.
  3. The theory: the biological model and the statistics behind it, with the assumptions each step makes.
  4. Commands: a worked example you can copy.
  5. Reading the output: which file or panel answers the question.
  6. Use cases: studies where the analysis fits.
  7. Cautions: how the result can mislead, and what to check before you believe it.
Page Analyses Synteny and collinearity homology search, filtering, chaining, quota alignment, dot plots, karyotype and local plots Ks and whole-genome duplications Ka/Ks, Ks distributions, mixture models, dating, WGDs on the species tree Subgenomes of polyploids homoeologous sets, k-mer phasing, repeats, consensus, fractionation, orthology across genomes, circos Evolutionary strata Ks along sex and mating-type chromosomes, changepoints Sex chromosomes sex-specific k-mers, depth, genotype models, phased haplotypes, RAD markers, combined regions Duplicated genes and gene conversion WGD, tandem, proximal, transposed and dispersed duplicates with any search engine; whole-gene and partial conversion Gene functions GO and KEGG pathway enrichment of gene sets Transposable elements intact LTR retrotransposons, insertion ages, annotation, LAI Pan-genomes, alignments and structural variants pan-genes, k-mer sketches, whole-genome alignment and format conversion, SVs, introgression and its region views Ancestral genomes and synteny networks ancestral karyotypes, adjacencies, synteny networks, clustering, phylogenomic profiles

docs.title: Cautions that apply everywhere
docs.text:
• Annotation quality sets the ceiling. Synteny, Ks, fractionation and orthology all count genes. Missing genes look like losses, split genes look like tandem duplicates, and transposon genes annotated as genes add false anchors. Check gene completeness (genome busco) before comparing genomes, and use annotations of similar quality.
  • Assembly errors look like rearrangements. A misjoin looks like a translocation, and a collapsed duplication looks like a gene loss. Confirm a surprising rearrangement with reads or a second assembly before you report it.
  • Gene names are not orthology. Synteny gives positional homologues. Orthology needs a species tree or a reference that branched off before the duplication.
  • Labels are arbitrary. Subgenome names, cluster numbers and mixture components are labels chosen by the method. Compare runs through their content (genes, positions), not through their names.
  • A P-value is not an effect size. With tens of thousands of genes almost any difference is significant. Report the size of the difference (retention, Ks, rate) next to the test.
  • Keep the record. Every command writes a .mcscan3 project file with its inputs, options and versions; mcscan3 cite prints what to cite.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: What did the chromosomes of an ancestor look like, which rearrangements produced today's karyotypes, and how are syntenic loci shared and lost across many genomes?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
Ancestral genomes (ancestral genomes, ancestral karyotype, ancestral tree-karyotype):

  1. Gene families (pan-genes or hierarchical orthogroups) link genes across species.
  2. Adjacencies (two families next to each other) are scored in every genome and placed on the species tree; an adjacency present in genomes on both sides of a node is inferred in that ancestor.
  3. Ancestral adjacencies are joined into contiguous ancestral regions (CARs), then into ancestral chromosomes.
  4. Each modern genome is painted with the ancestral chromosomes, which shows fusions, fissions and translocations along the tree.

Synteny networks (network build, network cluster, network profile, network tree):

  1. Every syntenic anchor pair from every pairwise comparison becomes an edge between two genes.
  2. The network is clustered (MCL by default; Leiden, Infomap, Louvain or connected components); a cluster is a syntenic locus shared by a set of genomes.
  3. Each cluster's presence and copy number per species form a phylogenomic profile; profiles give a species tree and show where loci arose and were lost (Dollo parsimony, network gainloss).

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Parsimony of adjacencies. Rearrangements break adjacencies. An adjacency seen in two lineages that split at a node most likely existed in their common ancestor, because forming the same adjacency twice independently is unlikely. Adjacencies that conflict (one family next to three others) are resolved by keeping the best-supported linear order.

Networks over pairwise blocks. Pairwise blocks become hard to combine for many genomes. A network keeps all evidence at once: genes in one cluster are linked by synteny directly or through other genomes. Loci gained in a clade, or lost in one lineage, show up as patterns in the profile matrix, which is why profiles carry phylogenetic signal (for example lineage-specific transpositions of genes into new contexts).

Clustering. MCL simulates random walks and keeps densely connected groups; its inflation parameter sets granularity. Leiden optimises modularity (or CPM) with guaranteed connected communities; Infomap compresses a description of random walks. On synteny networks MCL, Leiden and Infomap give similar locus-level clusters; network compare measures the agreement.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
mcscan3 pan genes grape peach poplar --ref grape --bed-dir data --anchors-dir synteny -o pan/pan
mcscan3 ancestral genomes species.nwk --families pan/pangenes.tsv --bed-dir data -o anc
mcscan3 ancestral karyotype anc.N2.cars.tsv --families pan/pangenes.tsv --bed-dir data -o N2 --format png
mcscan3 network build synteny/*.lifted.anchors -o net
mcscan3 network cluster net.edges.tsv -o net --method mcl
mcscan3 network profile net.clusters.tsv -o net --phylip
mcscan3 network tree net.profile.tsv -o net --method nj
mcscan3 network plot net --tree species.nwk --kind all -o net --format png

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• anc.<node>.cars.tsv: the ancestral regions of each node and their families.
  • Karyotype figures: modern chromosomes painted by ancestral chromosome.
  • net.clusters.tsv: one syntenic locus per cluster; net.profile.tsv: counts per species.
  • Network plots: the profile heatmap ordered by the tree, and gains and losses on the tree.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Reconstructing the ancestral karyotype of a family (for example the ancestral crucifer karyotype) and the rearrangements leading to each species.
  • Finding loci gained in one clade, such as lineage-specific gene clusters.
  • Building a species tree from synteny when gene trees disagree.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Ancestors depend on the sampling. An ancestor is inferred from its descendants; with few or closely related genomes, ancestral adjacencies are uncertain, and outgroups matter.
  • Polyploidy complicates adjacencies. Duplicated regions give each family two neighbourhoods; reconstruct before and after a WGD with care, or use one copy per region.
  • Order within CARs is surer than their joins. Joining CARs into chromosomes is the weakest step; treat ancestral chromosome counts as hypotheses.
  • Clustering parameters change cluster sizes. Report the method and its parameters; check important loci under a second method with network compare.
  • Profiles reflect annotation and assembly. A locus "lost" in one species may be unannotated or in a gap; losses on single terminal branches deserve the most suspicion.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: How did each duplicated gene arise: whole-genome duplication, tandem, proximal, transposed or dispersed duplication? Have paralogs from a shared polyploidy been homogenised by gene conversion since two species split?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
Duplication types (dup classify, and the dup step of pipeline run):

  1. Homologous pairs come from an all-against-all search of one genome. The search can be LAST, BLASTP, DIAMOND or MMseqs2 (pipeline run --search last|blast|diamond|mmseqs), or a tabular BLAST-format file you provide to dup classify.
  2. Each pair is assigned one class, in this order of priority:
  3. WGD: anchors of syntenic blocks within the genome;
  4. tandem: adjacent genes;
  5. proximal: on the same chromosome, at most --proximal-max genes apart;
  6. transposed: one copy at an ancestral locus (syntenic with an outgroup) and the other copy not;
  7. dispersed: all others.

Genes in no pair are singletons. With --unique, each gene counts in one class only.

Gene conversion (wgd conversion):

  1. Quartets. Two genomes A and B share a polyploidy older than their split. A quartet is a pair of syntenic paralogs in each genome (A1/A2, B1/B2), with A1–B1 and A2–B2 orthologs. Quartets are given in a file or built from three anchors files: paralogs of A, paralogs of B, and orthologs.
  2. Alignment. The four coding sequences are aligned on A1 (protein alignment, codons projected back). Ks is computed for all six pairs.
  3. Whole-gene conversion, I (WCV-I). In genome A, the paralogs are closer than either ortholog pair: Ks(A1, A2) < Ks(A1, B1) and Ks(A1, A2) < Ks(A2, B2). Support is the share of codon bootstrap replicates in which this holds.
  4. Whole-gene conversion, II (WCV-II). Stricter: the four-point condition must also favour ((A1, A2), (B1, B2)) over the expected ((A1, B1), (A2, B2)) and over ((A1, B2), (A2, B1)).
  5. Partial conversion (PCV). Sites are scored along the alignment:
  6. +1 where the paralogs of A share a base that one B ortholog has and the other lacks;
  7. −1 where the site shows the expected pattern A1 = B1 ≠ A2 = B2.

The highest-scoring segment is the converted tract. Its P value comes from shuffling the informative sites within each codon position. Where the tracts of A and B overlap, only the stronger one is kept.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
After a whole-genome duplication, the two copies of each gene diverge. When the species later splits, each gene has an ortholog in the other species that descends from the same copy. Without conversion, the gene tree is ((A1, B1), (A2, B2)), and paralogs are more divergent than orthologs.

Gene conversion copies sequence from one paralog onto the other, so the two become nearly identical. Conversion of the whole gene makes the paralogs of A closer than their orthologs, which inverts the expected Ks order. Conversion of a tract makes a run of sites where the paralogs of A agree and the orthologs disagree. This is the logic of Wang et al. (2009) for rice and sorghum, and of Wei et al. (2021) for rice subspecies.

Duplication types follow DupGen_finder (Qiao et al. 2019). Pairs inside syntenic blocks come from large duplications, adjacent pairs from unequal crossing-over, and transposed pairs from retrotransposition or DNA-based movement away from the ancestral locus.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# duplication types within the pipeline, with any search engine
mcscan3 pipeline run genomes/ -o run --search diamond --steps inputs,synteny,dup

# or from a self search and an outgroup search
mcscan3 dup classify grape.grape.last --bed grape.bed --outgroup grape.peach.last \
    --outgroup-bed peach.bed -o dup/grape

# gene conversion between two genomes sharing a WGD
mcscan3 wgd conversion A.cds B.cds -o conv/AB --paralogs-a A.A.anchors --paralogs-b B.B.anchors \
    --orthologs A.B.anchors --cpus 8 --format png

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• dup/<species>.<class>.pairs and <species>.genes (each gene's class).

The same grape and peach genes classified with each search engine. These are the test data: two grape chromosomes and one peach chromosome, with peach as the outgroup. Counts are of genes.

Grape genes LAST (CDS) BLASTP DIAMOND MMseqs2 WGD 1,225 1,645 1,558 1,630 tandem 421 336 354 354 proximal 187 164 168 160 transposed 338 193 244 209 dispersed 467 534 502 507 singleton 1,216 982 1,028 994

LAST on CDS finds fewer old WGD pairs than the protein searches, because nucleotide similarity between old paralogs is low.

  • conv/AB.tsv has one row per quartet: Ks of the six pairs, WCV-I and WCV-II support in each genome, and the PCV tract (codon start and end, score, P value and donor copy). conv/AB.json has the counts and percentages.
  • The figure plots paralog Ks against mean ortholog Ks for each genome. Points below the diagonal are whole-gene conversions (red); partial conversions are orange.

On 60 simulated quartets (20 unconverted, 20 with whole-gene conversion in A, 20 with a converted tract of 150 codons in A): - WCV-I and WCV-II found all 20 whole-gene conversions; - PCV found all 20 tracts; - nothing was called in genome B; - 3 of the 20 unconverted quartets were called partial conversions at P < 0.01.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Comparing duplication modes between species: tandem expansion of defence genes, retention of WGD copies of regulators.
  • The source of gene-family expansions found with bgc family or ortholog.
  • Conversion between homoeologs of crops sharing a polyploidy (rice subspecies, Brassica, cotton, wheat), and its effect on Ks-based dating.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• The search engine changes the counts. Sensitivity differs between LAST, BLASTP, DIAMOND and MMseqs2, and between CDS and proteins. Compare species with the same engine and settings.
  • Annotation errors make tandem duplicates. A gene split in two looks like a tandem pair, and fragmented assemblies break syntenic blocks into dispersed pairs.
  • Transposed needs a good outgroup. Without one (or with a distant one) no pair is called transposed, and those pairs are counted as dispersed.
  • Conversion detection needs the right quartets. Paralogs must come from a duplication older than the split of A and B, and the orthologs must be true orthologs (from synteny). A wrong ortholog turns the expected tree into an apparent conversion.
  • Partial conversion has false positives. In the simulation, 3 of 20 unconverted quartets were called at P < 0.01. Uneven substitution rates along a gene can cluster sites by chance. Treat single PCV calls as candidates, and look for tracts supported in both orthologs.
  • Conversion makes Ks too young. Converted paralogs give low Ks and can create false recent peaks in Ks distributions. Remove converted pairs before dating a WGD.
  • Saturation. Very old paralogs (Ks > 2) give unreliable Ks and few informative sites.

docs.title: How the methods decide: flowcharts
docs.text: Each chart traces one command from its inputs to its outputs, with every decision and every case where data is skipped or a run is stopped. The figures come from tools/showcase/flowcharts.py. Run python tools/showcase/flowcharts.py OUTDIR --format pdf for vector copies.

docs.title: The whole suite
docs.text: The work runs in four lanes. Synteny turns genomes into blocks; synteny blockinfo decides whether a block belongs to the event under study. Ancestral karyotypes paints genomes with an ancestral karyotype, calls the events, improves the ancestor and draws trajectories. Polyploidy lines up the copies of each event, measures biased loss and tests which copies are sisters. Networks grows a synteny network one genome at a time.

docs.title: synteny blockinfo
docs.text: Case What happens No BLAST table homo1–5 and tandem are empty; --max-tandem passes every block, but a --homo filter keeps none, so give the table when filtering by homo No Ks file, or no Ks in a block Ks columns are empty; a --ks filter leaves those blocks out A block fails any filter it stays in blockinfo.tsv with kept = 0 and is left out of <prefix>.anchors

docs.title: karyotype ancestor
docs.text: Case What happens A join or split in too few genomes, or cheaper as a lineage event it stays on its branch, and the ancestor is unchanged An ancestral join whose ends are already taken (not telomere-centric) reported as a conflict and not applied The ancestor changed run again with the new labels.tsv until nothing changes

docs.title: karyotype pindex
docs.text: Case What happens --bed given copies are compared by chromosome, so their identities are fixed and the result matches published values No --bed copies are compared by alignment column, with a warning: P is inflated because columns fill from the largest block first Either copy below --min-retention the window is skipped, since the region is probably missing from the assembly or the alignment |d| ≤ --diff a tie; it counts only with --with-ties P ≥ 0.3 biased loss: one copy dominant (allopolyploid-like) P < 0.3 balanced loss (autopolyploid-like)

docs.title: karyotype fusions
docs.text: Case What happens Fewer than --min-hits partners on either side unknown: the region is not in the target's anchors Both sides on one chromosome, within --max-gap genes shared: the target has the same fusion Partners on different chromosomes or far apart absent --tree each junction is placed at the common ancestor of the genomes sharing it, and called inconsistent if a genome below that node lacks it

docs.title: karyotype trees
docs.text: Case What happens Fewer than --min-genes genes with sequences the row is skipped --tree-tool nj built-in neighbour joining, with no external tools --tree-tool fasttree / iqtree used when installed; otherwise the command errors and names the tool

docs.title: network run
docs.text: Case What happens A new project every pair is compared (self pairs unless --no-self) Genomes added to the folder only pairs with a new genome are compared A genome file changed its checksum differs, so its pairs are compared again A genome removed its pairs are kept unless --drop-missing Different settings from the project refused, so one network never mixes parameters; --redo starts over Interrupted every finished pair is recorded in network.json; the next run resumes --only-build no comparisons: rebuild, cluster and report from the stored anchors

docs.title: Gene functions: GO and KEGG enrichment
The question
docs.text: Are genes of a set (retained after a polyploidy, in a syntenic region, lost from a subgenome, tandemly expanded) enriched for particular functions or pathways?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
1. Annotations.
  2. For GO (go enrich): gene-to-GO tables, plus the GO ontology (go-basic.obo).
  3. For KEGG (go kegg): gene-to-KO tables from eggNOG-mapper, KofamScan or KAAS, or KEGG link files.

KO-to-pathway tables are downloaded from the KEGG REST service once and cached (--kegg-dir). 2. Sets. A study set is tested against a population, which by default is all annotated genes. Use --sets to test several named sets at once, for example sets from go sets. 3. Test. One-sided Fisher's exact test for over-representation, corrected over the tested terms or pathways (--correction, BH by default). Pathways are tested only if they have between --min-genes and --max-genes genes. 4. KEGG filters. Global and overview maps are left out unless --overview is given. Human disease and drug maps are left out unless --all-categories is given. --org keeps only the pathways of a KEGG organism. 5. Output. A table, a dot plot of the top pathways, and links to KEGG maps with the study genes' KOs highlighted.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text: After a whole-genome duplication, genes are lost unevenly. Dosage-sensitive genes are retained in duplicate, because losing one copy unbalances a complex or a pathway. These include ribosomal proteins, proteasome subunits, respiratory complexes and transcription factors. Genes that work alone are usually returned to one copy, because extra copies are neutral or harmful. DNA repair and recombination genes are examples. This is the gene balance hypothesis (Birchler and Veitia). Enrichment tests ask whether such functional classes are over-represented among retained or lost genes.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# GO enrichment of genes kept in three copies after the Brassiceae triplication
mcscan3 go enrich --study three_copies.txt --population all.txt -a brapa.go.tsv --obo go-basic.obo -o go/brapa

# KEGG pathways of two named sets, with the Arabidopsis pathway list
mcscan3 go kegg -a ath.ko.tsv --sets sets.tsv --population pop.txt --org ath -o kegg/brapa_retention

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• <prefix>.kegg.tsv: set, pathway, counts in the study and population, fold enrichment, P and corrected P, and the KOs and genes behind each pathway.
  • <prefix>.links.tsv: a KEGG map link for each significant pathway, with the study KOs coloured.

Arabidopsis genes kept in three copies in B. rapa, against genes back to one copy (BH q < 0.05):

Set Pathway Fold q three copies Ribosome 1.99 1.1 × 10⁻¹⁰ three copies Oxidative phosphorylation 2.03 4.1 × 10⁻⁴ three copies Proteasome 2.47 1.7 × 10⁻³ three copies Glucosinolate metabolism 2.39 1.7 × 10⁻³ three copies Plant hormone signal transduction 1.40 5.4 × 10⁻³ one copy Homologous recombination 1.46 1.9 × 10⁻³ one copy Fanconi anemia pathway 1.72 2.6 × 10⁻³ one copy Base excision repair 1.58 0.018 one copy Mismatch repair 1.69 0.022 one copy Non-homologous end-joining 2.28 0.034

Dosage-sensitive complexes were kept in three copies, and DNA repair genes went back to one copy, as the gene balance hypothesis predicts.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Functions retained or lost after polyploidy, per subgenome or per WGD event.
  • Functions of genes in a region: a QTL, an introgression, a sex-determining region, a BGC.
  • Functions of tandemly expanded or species-specific genes.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• The population sets the answer. Test against the genes that could have been in the set, for example genes with a syntenic ortholog in the reference. Using the whole genome mixes in genes that could never be counted.
  • Annotation transfer is circular. If KOs or GO terms were transferred from Arabidopsis by similarity, conserved genes are more often annotated. Compare sets annotated the same way.
  • Pathways overlap. One complex can make several pathways significant (ribosome and its biogenesis; OXPHOS and metabolic overviews). Read the gene lists, not only the pathway names.
  • Disease maps are human. KEGG disease pathways (for example "Fanconi anemia") name human diseases but contain conserved genes, here DNA repair. They are off by default; read them as gene sets, not as diseases.
  • Fold, not only q. With thousands of genes small shifts become significant. Report the fold enrichment with the corrected P.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: When did the duplications in a genome happen, which of them were whole-genome duplications (WGDs), and where do they sit on the species tree?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
1. Ks of gene pairs. For every pair of duplicates (or orthologues), the coding sequences are aligned codon by codon and the synonymous distance Ks is estimated (ks kaks).
  2. A Ks distribution. Three kinds, from noisiest to cleanest: all paralogues of a genome (paranome), syntenic duplicate pairs (anchors), and one median per syntenic block.
  3. Peaks. A mixture model (Gaussian, lognormal or Bayesian, compared by BIC) or kernel density finds the components; each WGD adds one peak (wgd mix, wgd peaks).
  4. Placing and dating. Ortholog Ks between species gives the Ks of each speciation on the same scale; a WGD peak older than a split happened before it (wgd date, wgd consensus).

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Ks as a clock. Synonymous changes do not change the protein, so they are under weak selection and accumulate roughly with time: Ks ≈ 2 μ t for two copies separated t years ago at rate μ per site per year. Ka (non-synonymous) is constrained by selection; Ka/Ks < 1 means purifying selection, ≈ 1 neutrality, > 1 positive selection on average over the gene, which is rare.

Estimators. Counting methods (NG86, LPB93) count synonymous and non-synonymous sites and differences and correct for multiple hits; maximum likelihood (GY94, codeml) fits a codon model. They agree for Ks below about 1, and diverge as Ks approaches saturation.

Why peaks. Small-scale duplication happens all the time and the copies die quickly, which gives an L-shaped distribution: many young pairs, few old. A WGD creates thousands of pairs at once; their Ks spreads around the age of the event (the spread grows with age because of rate variation and estimation noise), so a peak sits on the L-shaped background. Anchor pairs remove most of the background, because small-scale duplicates are rarely in collinear blocks.

Mixture models. The distribution is fitted as a sum of components; BIC penalises extra components. Ks is right-skewed, so components are fitted on log Ks or as lognormals.

Dating. Converting Ks to years needs a rate. Rates differ between lineages (woody perennials evolve more slowly than annuals), so a WGD peak is best compared with ortholog Ks of the same species (rate-adjusted placement), and converted to years with calibrated splits.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
mcscan3 ks kaks grape.grape.anchors --cds grape.cds --method lpb93 --cpus 8 -o grape.kaks.tsv
mcscan3 wgd ksd grape.cds --anchors grape.grape.lifted.anchors -o grape.anchor.tsv --method lpb93 --cpus 8
mcscan3 wgd blocks grape.anchor.tsv -o grape.blocks.tsv --max-ks 3 --bed grape.bed
mcscan3 wgd mix grape.blocks.tsv --model all --plot grape.mix.pdf > grape.mix.tsv   # report on stdout
mcscan3 wgd date grape --tree species.nwk --ks-dir orthologs/ --peaks grape.mix.tsv -o grape.date
mcscan3 wgd transcriptome trinity.fasta -o sample --cpus 8 --format png    # no genome

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• ks kaks: one row per pair with Ka, Ks and Ka/Ks for each method.
  • wgd mix: the components of each model, the BIC of each, and the best model; the plot overlays the components on the histogram.
  • wgd date: the Ks of each speciation from the focal species, with bootstrap intervals, and where each WGD peak falls among them.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Showing that a genome had a WGD, and how many.
  • Ordering a WGD relative to speciation events (shared or lineage-specific).
  • Choosing duplicate pairs of one age, for example to study expression divergence after a WGD.
  • Screening transcriptomes of species without a genome for WGDs.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Saturation. Above Ks ≈ 2–3, values are unreliable for every method; old WGDs merge into the tail. Use --max-ks and do not read peaks beyond it.
  • Not every peak is a WGD. Mixture models can split one skewed peak into two, and a burst of small-scale duplication can make a bump. Support a WGD with synteny (parallel blocks, depth) and, if possible, with gene trees (wgd consensus).
  • Not every WGD makes a peak. Old WGDs, or WGDs followed by heavy gene loss, can leave too few pairs. Absence of a peak is weak evidence.
  • Rate variation. The same Ks does not mean the same age in two lineages. Compare WGD peaks with ortholog Ks of the same species, not across species.
  • Gene conversion between homoeologues lowers their Ks, which makes a WGD look younger.
  • Paranome counting. Families with many members create many pairs; MCscan3 counts each duplication once (weights) to avoid this, which matters when you compare with other tools.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: What do several genomes of one species (or genus) share and what does each add? Which large differences (inversions, translocations, duplications, insertions and deletions) separate two assemblies, and which parts of a genome came from another lineage?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
Pan-genes (pan genes, pan run --mode gene): genes of every genome are grouped through synteny with a reference and with each other. Each group is a pan-gene, placed on the reference order. Groups present in every genome are core, in most soft-core, in some dispensable, in one private. Accumulation curves show how many new genes each added genome brings.

Sequence pan-genome (pan run --mode sequence): k-mer sketches of the assemblies (one k-mer in --scaled kept) give the same classes and curves without annotation.

Whole-genome alignment (wga align, wga chain): minimap2 aligns two assemblies base by base; colinear alignments are chained into DNA-level synteny blocks. wga convert converts alignments between PAF, MAF and UCSC chain, exactly (CIGAR-level, both strands), with length, identity and primary-only filters. wga stats reports reference and query coverage, identity, SNPs, indels and alignment span N50.

Structural variants (sv call, sv merge, sv pan): from the chained alignments, syntenic regions are separated from inversions (reverse-strand blocks between syntenic flanks), translocations (blocks out of order, or on another chromosome), duplications (regions aligned twice) and indels; SNPs and small indels come from the CIGAR strings. sv merge joins many genomes against one reference into pan-SVs with presence and absence.

Introgression (introgress scan): each window of a target genome is compared with source genomes or reads through k-mer containment; a hidden Markov model with a switch penalty paints each window with its best source. introgress plot paints whole chromosomes; introgress view draws chosen regions as genome-browser views (with genomeview): containment per source, the painted blocks, genes, aligned reads and any other window track, such as the combined score of sex run.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
A single reference misses sequence that other individuals carry. Gene content varies through presence/absence variation, which is common in plants because of transposons and incomplete purging after polyploidy. Accumulation curves fitted with Heaps' law (new genes ∝ N−α) tell an open pan-genome (α < 1, each new genome keeps adding genes) from a closed one.

Structural variants are defined relative to alignments: a region is syntenic when it aligns in order and orientation with its flanks. Only rearrangements whose flanks align on both sides can be called reliably, which is why repeats and gaps limit SV calling.

k-mer containment estimates sequence identity: if a fraction c of a window's k-mers is found in a source, identity is about c1/k. Painting compares sources window by window; the switch penalty keeps one source over long runs, as expected for introgressed tracts, rather than flipping on noise.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
mcscan3 pan genes grape peach poplar --ref grape --bed-dir data --anchors-dir synteny -o pan/pan
mcscan3 pan run g1.fa g2.fa g3.fa --mode sequence -o pan/seq
mcscan3 wga align col.fa ler.fa --preset asm5 -o wga/col.ler
mcscan3 wga chain wga/col.ler.paf -o wga/col.ler
mcscan3 wga convert wga/col.ler.paf wga/col.ler.maf --ref col.fa --qry ler.fa --primary
mcscan3 wga stats wga/col.ler.paf --primary -o wga/col.ler
mcscan3 sv call wga/col.ler.paf --ref col.fa --qry ler.fa -o sv/col.ler
mcscan3 sv plot sv/col.ler.sv.tsv -o sv/col.ler.stack --min-size 20000
mcscan3 introgress scan target.fa --source parentA.fa --source parentB.fa --window 50000 -o intro/target
mcscan3 introgress view intro/target -o intro/target.view.png --top 3 --bed target.bed

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• pangenes.tsv: one pan-gene per row, its genes in each genome, its class; the curves and the Heaps' fit in the report.
  • .sv.tsv: one variant per row with type, positions on both genomes and size.
  • wga stats: on Arabidopsis Col-0 against Ler, 7,028 primary alignments covered 87.6% of the Col-0 reference at identity 0.9763, with 604,672 SNPs. The same alignments round-trip PAF → MAF → PAF and PAF → chain with identical coordinates and matches.
  • The introgression painting: the best source of each window along each chromosome.
  • The introgression view: one panel per region. Below are the two longest non-background blocks of Quercus pubescens against four other oaks.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Finding genes absent from the reference but present in other cultivars (resistance genes are a common case).
  • Calling inversions that suppress recombination in crosses, or that carry adaptive alleles.
  • Mapping introgressed segments from a wild relative in a breeding line.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Absent or not annotated? A gene missing from one genome's annotation may still be in its sequence. Confirm presence/absence on the assembly (pan run --mode sequence, or by aligning the gene).
  • Annotation differences inflate private genes. Genomes annotated by different pipelines disagree on gene models; annotate together when you can.
  • Repeats and gaps hide SVs. Breakpoints inside long repeats or assembly gaps cannot be placed; the size of the smallest reliable SV depends on assembly quality.
  • Collapsed duplications in one assembly look like deletions relative to the other.
  • Introgression versus shared ancestry. A window that matches a source best can be shared ancestral variation (incomplete lineage sorting) rather than introgression; use sources from several lineages, and look for long tracts.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: Does a species have genetic sex determination? If so, is it XY (males heterogametic) or ZW (females heterogametic), which chromosome carries the sex-determining region, and where on it does the region start and end?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
MCscan3 reads several kinds of evidence. Each has its own command, and sex run combines whatever data you have:

Command Data Signal of sex linkage sex kmers whole-genome reads of several males and females k-mers found in (nearly) every individual of one sex and in none of the other sex coverage the same reads and a reference male:female read depth away from 1 sex vcf genotypes (VCF) of sexed individuals, from any caller, RAD-seq or whole-genome sites that fit XY, ZW or hemizygous inheritance; FST between the sexes; heterozygosity of each sex sex haplotypes a phased assembly of the heterogametic sex k-mers of one haplotype missing from the other sex rad RAD-seq reads, no reference needed markers present in one sex and not the other sex run any combination the evidence above on shared windows, combined sex simulate none a population with sex chromosomes of known structure, for testing
  1. Sex-specific k-mers. Each read set is reduced to a sample of its k-mers (one in --scaled) with counts. K-mers seen fewer than --min-count times are dropped as sequencing errors. A k-mer in at least --frac of the males and in no female is male-specific. If male-specific k-mers far outnumber female-specific ones, the system is XY; the reverse means ZW.
  2. Depth. The k-mers that occur once in the reference are looked up in every sample's counts and divided by the sample's median, so samples of any depth compare. Each window gets log2 of male:female depth.
  3. Genotype models. For every SNP, the genotype counts of females and males are fitted under five models: autosomal, XY, X-hemizygous, ZW and Z-hemizygous. Each model allows a genotyping error rate. BIC weights give each site's probability of sex linkage.
  4. Haplotypes. In an assembly of an XY male, the X and Y differ along the non-recombining region, while autosome haplotypes differ only at heterozygous sites. The share of k-mers of hap1 missing from hap2 rises along the sex-determining region.
  5. RAD markers. The first bases of each read are a marker. Each marker is tested for presence by sex (Fisher's exact test, Bonferroni or BH correction). With few individuals no marker passes, so markers in most of one sex and none of the other are counted too.
  6. Combination (sex run). Each signal is oriented for the system:
  7. k-mers specific to the heterogametic sex;
  8. |log2 M:F| depth;
  9. sex-linked SNPs of that system's type;
  10. FST;
  11. |log2| of the heterozygosity ratio.

Each signal becomes a robust z-score (median and MAD) over all windows. A window's combined score is the mean z of the evidence available there. Windows scoring at least --min-score are joined into regions. The system is the majority call of the evidence, unless --system sets it.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Sex chromosomes arise when an autosome gains a sex-determining gene and recombination around it stops. The non-recombining copy (Y or W) is then present in only one sex and evolves on its own.

  • It diverges. Every mutation on it is fixed against the X (or Z). In males, X/Y differences look like heterozygous sites, so males are heterozygous where females are not. Allele frequencies also differ between the sexes, which raises FST.
  • It gains sequence, such as insertions and transposons, that the X lacks. That sequence gives k-mers found only in males.
  • It loses sequence. Where the Y lost genes, males carry one X: half the female depth (log2 M:F = −1), with no heterozygosity there.

In a ZW species every signal is mirrored between the sexes. These signals come from different data and fail in different ways (see the cautions), so agreement between them is stronger evidence than any one alone. Young sex chromosomes show little divergence and few specific k-mers, and old ones may have lost most of the Y. Combining the evidence covers both cases better.

The genotype models follow SDpop (Käfer et al. 2021). Sex-specific k-mers follow Akagi et al. (2014) and later k-mer workflows. Depth and heterozygosity scans follow findZX (Sigeman et al. 2022) and SexFindR (Grayson et al. 2022). RAD markers follow RADSex (Feron et al. 2021). Haplotype-specific k-mers follow SCINKD.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# a test population: 6 males, 6 females, five 200 kb chromosomes, XY on chr1
mcscan3 sex simulate sim --system XY

# every line of evidence at once
mcscan3 sex run -o sex/sim -r sim/reference.fa -s sim/samples.tsv --vcf sim/genotypes.vcf \
    --rad sim/rad_samples.tsv -w 10000 --cache sex/kmers --format png

# or one at a time
mcscan3 sex kmers -s samples.tsv -r reference.fa -o sex/k --reads-out sex/y_reads.fa
mcscan3 sex coverage -s samples.tsv -r reference.fa -o sex/c
mcscan3 sex vcf genotypes.vcf -s samples.tsv -o sex/v
mcscan3 sex haplotypes hap1.fa hap2.fa -o sex/h
mcscan3 sex rad -s rad_samples.tsv -o sex/r

samples.tsv has one line per individual: name<TAB>M|F<TAB>reads[,reads]. For sex vcf, the names must match the VCF columns and the reads column can be left out. --cache keeps each sample's k-mer counts between runs.

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• <prefix>.json: the system, the call of each evidence, the candidate chromosome and the regions.
  • <prefix>.regions.tsv: each region, its score and the evidence above the threshold in it.
  • <prefix>.windows.tsv: every raw signal, its z-score and the combined score, per window.
  • The figure has one track per evidence plus the combined score, along the genome, with called regions shaded.

On the simulated XY population (6 males, 6 females, 8× coverage), the sex-determining region was placed at chr1:60,000–150,000, exactly the simulated region. The system came out XY from k-mers, depth and genotypes. - k-mers: 3,185 male-specific against 11 female-specific sampled k-mers. - Genotypes: 2,964 of 6,843 SNPs were sex-linked: 2,922 XY-type and 42 ZW-type. - Haplotypes: sex haplotypes ranked chr1 first, with a robust z of 182. - RAD: of 10,788 markers, none passed Bonferroni with only 12 individuals. But 52 markers were male-specific and none female-specific, which also gives XY.

In the ZW simulation every evidence called ZW (3,248 female-specific against 17 male-specific k-mers) and found the same region.

The windows where the simulated Y lost a stretch show the deficit side of the heterozygosity signal: males are hemizygous there. This is why the combined score uses |log2|.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Finding the sex system and the sex chromosome of a species with no prior information, from a few sexed individuals (dioecious plants, fish, reptiles, insects).
  • Placing the sex-determining region on a new assembly before studying its genes.
  • Getting sex-linked markers for sexing seedlings or juveniles (sex rad, sex kmers --reads-out).
  • Choosing the region and the X-Y gene pairs for ks strata, which finds evolutionary strata.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Sample size. With few individuals per sex, a k-mer or SNP can look sex-specific by chance, and no RAD marker survives correction. Use at least 5 to 10 individuals of each sex. Accept a call only when several kinds of evidence agree.
  • Sexing errors. One mis-sexed individual removes most sex-specific k-mers and markers, because they must be absent from every individual of the other sex. Lower --frac or check sexes if evidence is weak.
  • Population structure. If the males and females come from different populations, FST and allele frequencies differ between the sexes genome-wide. Sample both sexes from the same places.
  • The reference sex matters. A reference assembled from the homogametic sex has no Y or W. Its male-specific k-mers are then counted as unplaced, and depth shows only the X (male depth halved). A heterogametic reference shows Y-specific contigs directly.
  • Young or small regions give weak signals: little divergence, few specific k-mers, normal depth. Use smaller windows and genotype evidence, and expect a region of a few windows.
  • Repeats inflate k-mer and depth signals. Windows full of satellites or recent transposons can score high on depth alone. Check that a region is supported by more than one evidence (the evidence column).
  • Environmental or polygenic sex determination leaves no region. An empty result with many individuals is evidence against a simple XY or ZW system, not proof.
  • Hemizygous genes (X-hemizygous model) need care. Males homozygous at every site also arise from low coverage or allele dropout in RAD data. Look at depth before reading them as Y gene loss.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: On a pair of sex chromosomes (X/Y, Z/W, U/V) or mating-type chromosomes, did recombination stop all at once or in steps, and where are the steps?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
1. Gametologues. Pairs of genes, one on each chromosome of the pair, that descend from one ancestral gene. Reciprocal best hits between the two chromosomes, or synteny when the two haplotypes are still collinear.
  2. Ks of each pair (ks kaks).
  3. Order. The pairs are laid along the gene order of one chromosome, or better, of an ancestral genome (an outgroup where the region is still autosomal), with --ref-anchors.
  4. Changepoints (ks strata): for 0 to --max-changepoints changepoints, the exact best division of the series into strata, each with its own mean and variance of Ks.
  5. Model choice and support: BIC chooses the number of strata and gives BIC weights; a residual bootstrap gives 95% intervals for each changepoint; adjacent strata are compared with a one-sided Mann-Whitney test.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Once recombination stops between two chromosomes in a region, the two copies of each gene in that region evolve independently and their Ks grows with time. If recombination stopped in several steps (for example through successive inversions on the Y), each step leaves a block of genes with a similar Ks: an evolutionary stratum. Older strata have higher Ks. Lahn and Page (1999) found four strata along the human X this way.

The segmentation assumes Ks is constant within a stratum apart from noise, and that noise grows with Ks (older pairs vary more), so each stratum has its own variance. The best division for a given number of changepoints is found exactly by dynamic programming; BIC trades fit against the number of parameters (a mean and a variance per stratum, plus the changepoints).

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# gametologue pairs (reciprocal best hits between the X and Y CDS), then their Ks
mcscan3 ks kaks XY.anchors --cds XY.cds -o XY.kaks.tsv
# strata along the X, in its own order
mcscan3 ks strata XY.kaks.tsv --bed X.bed --chrom X --max-changepoints 5 --min-size 2 -o human_XY
# along an ancestral genome instead, with one chromosome reversed
mcscan3 ks strata hap.kaks.tsv --bed anc.bed --ref-anchors anc.hap1.anchors --chrom chr3 --chrom chr7- -o strata

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• .strata.tsv: every pair with its position and stratum.
  • .strata.segments.tsv: each stratum's pairs, mean and median Ks, the changepoint interval and the test against the next stratum.
  • .strata.models.tsv: BIC and weight of every number of changepoints.
  • The figure: Ks along the chromosome coloured by stratum, the stratum means, the bootstrap intervals as bars below the points, and the BIC curve.

On the 18 human X/Y gametologue pairs found from the Ensembl annotation, the oldest stratum (SOX3/SRY, RBMX/RBMY, HSFX1/HSFY1; mean Ks 1.72) lies on distal Xq and the youngest (NLGN4X/Y, VCX/VCY; mean Ks 0.08) on distal Xp, as in the published strata. With so few pairs only three strata are resolved, and the intervals are wide.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Sex chromosomes of plants and animals (papaya, Silene, willow, birds, mammals).
  • Mating-type chromosomes of fungi (for example anther-smut fungi), where strata are common.
  • Supergenes and other non-recombining regions.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• The order matters most. Strata are contiguous only in the ancestral order. Rearrangements on the chromosome you use as the order (for example the X-transposed region of the human X) break strata into pieces or mix them. Use an outgroup in which the region is autosomal when you can, and reverse or reorder chromosomes with --chrom.
  • Wrong pairs make false strata. A paralogue taken as a gametologue has the wrong Ks (in the human example AP1S2/TMSB4Y and TSPYL2/TSPY4 are such outliers). Check outlying pairs before reading a small stratum.
  • Gene conversion and recurrent recombination near the boundary lower Ks and blur steps.
  • Saturation: in very old strata Ks saturates, so differences between old strata shrink.
  • Few pairs, little power. With tens of pairs, BIC may choose fewer strata than exist, and the intervals can span several genes. A changepoint is a position in gene order, not a base-pair breakpoint.
  • Gradual is possible. A smooth gradient of Ks can be cut into steps by any segmentation; look at the BIC weights and at whether the steps are sharp in the plot.

docs.title: The question
