docs.text: A polyploid carries two or more sets of chromosomes (subgenomes). Which chromosomes belong together, which progenitor each set came from, did one subgenome lose more genes than the others, and which copies in related polyploids are orthologous subgenome by subgenome?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
subgenome phase runs the whole chain; each step is also its own command.

  1. Homoeologous sets (subgenome homoeologs): chromosomes (or segments) that are copies of one ancestral chromosome, from self-synteny (--self) or from synteny with an unduplicated relative (--ref).
  2. Differential k-mers (subgenome kmer): short sequences far more common on one member of each homoeologous set than on the others. Chromosomes are clustered by these k-mers, constrained so that two members of one set never fall in the same subgenome; bootstrap gives support.
  3. Repeats (subgenome repeats): intact LTR retrotransposons that carry the subgenome-specific k-mers, with their insertion ages.
  4. Homology and Ks to progenitors (subgenome assign): when relatives of the progenitors are sequenced, each gene votes for its closest progenitor genome.
  5. Consensus (subgenome consensus): all lines of evidence matched to one set of names, per chromosome and along it, with homoeologous exchanges kept only when two lines agree.
  6. Retention (subgenome retention): genes kept by each phased subgenome, and a sign test of biased fractionation.
  7. Circos (subgenome circos): every line of evidence on one circle.

subgenome orthology answers a different question: across several genomes that share one polyploidy, which copies are orthologous subgenome by subgenome.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Allopolyploids and progenitor-specific repeats. An allopolyploid forms from two (or more) diverged species. While those progenitors were separate, each accumulated its own bursts of transposable elements and satellite repeats. These repeats are spread over all chromosomes of that progenitor, so after the merger the chromosomes of one subgenome share k-mers that the others lack. This is why k-mers phase subgenomes without any progenitor genome. The LTR retrotransposons that carry them can be dated (the two LTRs of an element are identical at insertion), and elements inserted before the merger date the time the progenitors were apart.

Fractionation and its bias. After a WGD most duplicate genes return to single copy by losing one copy. In many allopolyploids losses are biased: one subgenome keeps more genes (least fractionated, LF) and is often more highly expressed (subgenome dominance). The usual explanation is that the progenitors differed in transposon load near genes, which lowered expression and made genes of one subgenome more dispensable. A sign test compares regions where only one of two subgenomes kept the gene.

Orthology across genomes sharing a polyploidy. After a WGD shared by several species, each gene of an unduplicated reference has a pillar: its surviving copies in each species, one slot per homoeologous track. Which slot of species A matches which slot of species B is unknown. subgenome orthology fits three things together:

  • a loss model on the species tree: at the WGD each pillar has all k copies; along each branch copies are lost one at a time, subgenome s at a rate proportional to ws (unequal w is biased fractionation), and the last copy is never lost;
  • a hidden Markov model along the reference, whose hidden state is how the slots of every species map to the subgenomes. Neighbouring pillars keep the same state unless synteny breaks (probability θ), because whole blocks were inherited together;
  • maximum likelihood for the branch lengths (losses per gene), w and θ. The forward-backward algorithm gives each pillar's posterior, and a second fit with equal w gives a likelihood-ratio test of biased fractionation.

Biased loss is what tells the subgenomes apart: without it, the labels of the subgenomes can be swapped without changing the likelihood.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
# phase a hexaploid from itself (Camelina sativa)
mcscan3 ortholog run csat csat --cpus 8
mcscan3 ks kaks csat.csat.lifted.anchors --cds csat.cds -o csat.kaks.tsv --cpus 8
mcscan3 subgenome phase csat.dna.fa.gz --bed csat.bed --self csat.csat.lifted.anchors --copies 3 \
    --cpus 8 -o phase/csat
mcscan3 subgenome circos phase/csat --bed csat.bed --anchors csat.csat.lifted.anchors \
    --ks csat.kaks.tsv --key right -o csat.circos.pdf

# orthology across two species sharing the Brassiceae triplication, Arabidopsis as reference
mcscan3 ortholog run ath brapa --quota 1:3
mcscan3 ortholog run ath bole --quota 1:3
mcscan3 subgenome orthology --ref-bed ath.bed --copies 3 \
    --genome brapa=ath.brapa.lifted.1x3.anchors:brapa.bed \
    --genome bole=ath.bole.lifted.1x3.anchors:bole.bed -o brassica

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• <prefix>.phase.md: one report with every step.
  • <prefix>.consensus.tsv: the subgenome of each chromosome and its support; .consensus.exchanges.tsv: homoeologous exchanges backed by two lines of evidence.
  • <prefix>.retention.tsv and .retention.pairs.tsv: genes kept per subgenome and the bias tests.
  • brassica.orthology.tsv: per pillar, the genes of each subgenome (LF, MF1, MF2) in each species and the posterior; brassica.orthology.json: the loss weights, branch lengths, θ and the test.

In the Brassiceae example, LF kept 75.7% of 22,021 pillars in B. rapa, MF1 52.1% and MF2 32.3%, and most losses (0.59 per gene) happened before B. rapa and B. oleracea split (0.12 and 0.11 after).

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Naming the subgenomes of a new allopolyploid assembly, with or without progenitor genomes.
  • Testing subgenome dominance: biased retention here, then expression of the phased homoeologues.
  • Dating when the progenitors were apart and when they merged (LTR ages, Ks of homoeologues).
  • Matching homoeologues across several species that share a polyploidy, as input for gene-tree, expression or selection studies by subgenome.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• Autopolyploids have no progenitor-specific repeats. The k-mer step finds no differential k-mers or noise; phasing then rests on synteny and fractionation alone, and "subgenome" may not be a meaningful unit.
  • Old polyploids erode the signal. Repeats decay and are purged over millions of years. In the Camelina sativa run one subgenome had no specific k-mers at all; MCscan3 says so and draws no exchanges for it, rather than forcing a call.
  • Names are labels. "SG1" in one run need not be "SG1" in another. LF/MF names in subgenome orthology are given after the fit, by retention.
  • Exchanges need two lines of evidence. A single k-mer window can flip by chance; MCscan3 keeps an exchange only when two independent lines agree. Assembly switch errors between homoeologues can still look like exchanges.
  • Retention depends on the reference. Genes the reference lacks, or misses in its annotation, are invisible. Retention from self-synteny (no reference) cannot see genes lost from all copies.
  • Orthology posteriors. A pillar where both species kept the same single copy is easy; a pillar where each species kept a different copy is ambiguous, and its posterior is lower. Filter on the posterior (for example ≥ 0.95) for downstream use. The model assumes copies are lost one at a time and never regained, and that the track a block sits on is correct; large rearrangements after the WGD that move only part of a block can mislead it.
  • Significance with many genes. The bias test is almost always significant with thousands of pillars; the loss weights and the retention percentages are the effect sizes to report.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: Which regions of two genomes descend from the same ancestral region, and in what order and orientation? Synteny here means conserved gene order (collinearity), not only being on the same chromosome.

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
1. Homology search. All proteins (or CDS) of one genome are compared with all of the other (LAST by default; DIAMOND, MMseqs2 or BLAST optionally).
  2. Filtering. Hits are kept when they are strong relative to each gene's best hit (C-score), and tandem arrays (runs of neighbouring homologous genes) are collapsed to one representative, so one array does not create a stack of anchors.
  3. Chaining. Hits are placed on a grid of gene ranks. Chains of hits that run in a line, with small gaps, are joined by dynamic programming into blocks. A hit inside a block is an anchor.
  4. Lifting. Hits near a block that the filter dropped are added back (.lifted.anchors).
  5. Quota alignment (optional). When genome B had a duplication the other did not, each region of A should match up to n regions of B. Quota alignment keeps the best set of blocks with at most m copies on one side and n on the other (--quota m:n), solved as an integer program.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Gene order decays by rearrangements (inversions, translocations, fusions, fissions) and by gene loss and gain. Two genomes keep long collinear runs when few rearrangements separate them. A run of k homologous gene pairs in the same order is very unlikely by chance when the genes are many, so chaining with a gap limit separates real blocks from scattered paralogue hits. The gap limit and the minimum block size set the balance between sensitivity (old, eroded blocks) and false blocks.

After a whole-genome duplication (WGD), every region exists twice, then genes are lost from one copy or the other (fractionation). A self comparison of a polyploid therefore shows parallel blocks, and a comparison with an unduplicated relative shows each region of the relative matching 2 (or 3, ...) regions of the polyploid. The depth of synteny (synteny depth) estimates that ratio, which is the quota to use.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
mcscan3 ortholog run grape peach --cpus 8                 # search, filter, chain, lift
mcscan3 synteny depth grape.poplar.anchors --histogram    # how many poplar copies per grape region
mcscan3 ortholog run grape poplar --quota 1:2             # poplar had a WGD that grape did not
mcscan3 plot dotplot grape.poplar.lifted.anchors --theme mcscan3
mcscan3 plot karyotype --genomes grape,peach,poplar --anchors-dir . --theme mcscan3

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• <a>.<b>.anchors and .lifted.anchors: blocks separated by ###, one anchor pair per line.
  • The dot plot: diagonal runs are blocks; anti-diagonals are inversions; parallel runs on one side are duplicated regions.
  • synteny depth: a peak at 2 for poplar regions per grape region means one extra WGD in poplar.
  • The karyotype plot links blocks between chromosome bars of several genomes.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Finding orthologous regions to transfer annotation or markers between species.
  • Showing a WGD (parallel blocks) or a chromosome fusion (one chromosome matching two).
  • Choosing gene pairs for Ks (anchors are cleaner than all paralogues).
  • The first step of nearly every other analysis in MCscan3.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• A missing block is not proof of a rearrangement. It can come from a poor annotation, a gap in the assembly, or a block too eroded for the gap limit.
  • Old duplications fade. Blocks from ancient WGDs (for example the gamma triplication of core eudicots) are short and few; lowering --min-size finds more of them, and more false ones.
  • Quota choice changes the answer. Too low a quota drops real paralogous blocks; too high keeps blocks from older duplications. Use synteny depth and the known history of the clade.
  • Tandem duplicates are collapsed for chaining; study them separately with dup classify.
  • Anchors are homologues, not necessarily orthologues. In a polyploid, the best anchor in one block can be an out-paralogue. ortholog soi keeps blocks supported by orthologues from OrthoFinder or reciprocal best hits.

docs.title: The question
docs.text: Which transposable elements (TEs) does a genome carry, how much of it do they make up, when were they active, and how complete is the assembly of its repeats?

docs.title: The logic
docs.text:
1. Structural search for intact elements.
  2. te ltr: LTR retrotransposons, found as two long terminal repeats a few kb apart, flanked by a target-site duplication (TSD) and bounded by the TG...CA motif.
  3. te tir: DNA transposons, found as terminal inverted repeats with a TSD.
  4. te helitron: Helitrons, found by their ends and hairpin.
  5. Classification (te classify): protein domains of each element (reverse transcriptase, integrase, ...) searched with HMMs put it into a superfamily and clade.
  6. Library (te library): the elements are reduced to a non-redundant set of family sequences.
  7. Whole-genome annotation (te annotate): RepeatMasker with that library finds every copy, intact or fragmented, and summarises the TE content by class.
  8. Ages (te age): insertion times of intact LTR elements, solo-LTR to intact ratios, and activity through time per clade.
  9. LAI (te lai): the LTR Assembly Index, the share of LTR sequence that sits in intact elements, corrected for the age of the elements.

docs.title: The theory
docs.text:
Dating LTR retrotransposons. When an LTR retrotransposon inserts, its two LTRs are copied from one template and are identical. Afterwards each LTR mutates independently, so the divergence d between the two LTRs grows with time: t = d / (2 r), where r is the neutral substitution rate per site per year (--rate, 1.3 × 10⁻⁸ by default, a common grass value). A correction for multiple hits (Kimura) is applied to d.

Solo LTRs. Unequal recombination between the two LTRs of one element removes the internal region and leaves one LTR. A high solo-to-intact ratio means a lineage removes elements efficiently.

Why LAI measures assembly quality. Intact LTR elements are long and repetitive, so short-read assemblies break them into fragments. The more intact LTR sequence an assembly holds, relative to all LTR sequence, the more continuous its repeats are. Genomes with very young or very old elements are corrected through the mean LTR identity.

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
mcscan3 te ltr genome.fa --cpus 8 -o te/genome                       # intact LTR retrotransposons
mcscan3 te classify te/genome.ltr.fa --ltr te/genome.ltr.tsv -o te/genome.cls
mcscan3 te tir genome.fa -o te/genome                                # DNA transposons
mcscan3 te helitron genome.fa -o te/genome
mcscan3 te library te/genome.ltrlib.fa te/genome.tir.fa te/genome.helitron.fa \
    --ltr te/genome.ltr.tsv -o te/genome
mcscan3 te annotate genome.fa --library te/genome.telib.fa --cpus 8 -o te/genome.ann
mcscan3 te age te/genome.ltr.tsv -a te/genome.ann.te.tsv -o te/genome
mcscan3 te lai genome.fa --intact te/genome.ltr.tsv -a te/genome.ann.te.tsv -o te/genome

docs.title: Reading the output
docs.text:
• <prefix>.ltr.tsv: one intact element per row, with LTR identity, TSD, motif and age.
  • <prefix>.ann.te.summary.tsv: genome share of every class and superfamily.
  • <prefix>.age.tsv and its figure: insertion ages per clade, recent bursts, solo:intact ratios.
  • <prefix>.lai.json: raw and corrected LAI for the genome, and regional LAI in windows.

docs.title: Use cases
docs.text:
• Annotating repeats of a new assembly before gene annotation.
  • Comparing TE bursts between species or subgenomes (with subgenome repeats).
  • Judging assembly quality next to gene completeness (LAI above about 10 is often called reference quality, above 20 gold quality).
  • Dating events in genome history, such as when the progenitors of an allopolyploid were apart.

docs.title: Cautions
docs.text:
• The rate sets the clock. Ages scale with 1/r. A rate from another lineage can be off several fold; report the rate with the ages, and compare ages between species only with one rate each.
  • Gene conversion between LTRs makes elements look younger; nested insertions can be mistaken for one element if the search is careless (MCscan3 reports nesting).
  • Old elements are invisible. Elements older than a few million years decay and stop being recognised as intact, so age distributions are biased toward young elements; a peak of young insertions is not proof of a recent burst.
  • Library quality drives annotation. Families missing from the library are missed by RepeatMasker; a curated library or several detection methods help.
  • LAI depends on the TE landscape. Genomes with few LTR elements give unstable LAI; compare LAI between assemblies of the same species rather than across distant species.
